profiles.meeting_scenario: The Department of Urology at a teaching hospital is planning a 45-minute CME grand rounds session titled "A Primer on Clinical Trial Design" for practicing urologists. The session is scheduled for next month and must appeal to attending physicians and senior residents while fitting the hospital's standard grand rounds workflow. This planning meeting is between the physician faculty lead and the surgical education coordinator to decide the session structure, supporting materials, ownership of each component, and the internal submission timeline. The agenda is to align on what the primer should cover, what the "handout" and examples will look like, who will prepare the slide deck and accompanying materials, and what must be delivered by Friday. The expected outcome is a practical plan for producing the lecture deck, audience materials, and review package in time for circulation.

members.name: Dr. Elena Marquez
members.role: Associate Professor of Urology and Grand Rounds Faculty Lead
members.expertise: Clinical trials in urologic oncology, evidence appraisal, academic lecturing
members.background: Dr. Marquez leads investigator-initiated studies in bladder and prostate cancer and regularly teaches residents how to read trial papers critically; she is comfortable building high-yield teaching talks but usually relies on lean, content-first materials rather than formalized education packets.
members.private_state: She wants the session to feel practical for busy clinicians, limit prep time to what she can do around clinic, and avoid getting drawn into packaging tasks she sees as secondary to the educational message.
hidden_assumptions: A "primer" for practicing urologists should be selective and high-yield, not a point-by-point tour through every standard trial-design topic.
A "handout" is the learner-facing takeaway she provides to attendees, usually a concise summary or annotated slide printout rather than a broader assembled packet.
When someone asks for "case examples," the natural thing is to use published urology trials as illustrative examples of good or flawed design choices.
If materials are due "Friday," the key expectation is that the substantive content exists by then, even if polishing and assembly happen afterward.

members.name: Sarah Liu
members.role: CME Program Coordinator for Surgical Education
members.expertise: Grand rounds planning, educational materials workflow, faculty submission management
members.background: Sarah coordinates recurring surgical education sessions, works with faculty to turn talk ideas into standard grand rounds materials, and is used to assembling slide decks, audience handouts, objectives, and references into a single package for internal circulation; she is not a trialist but has developed a strong sense of what a complete methods-oriented session usually includes.
members.private_state: She wants to collect everything early enough that the session can move smoothly through the usual internal workflow, minimize back-and-forth with faculty late in the process, and make sure attendees receive a polished, self-contained set of materials.
hidden_assumptions: A session billed as a "primer" should visibly touch all the core trial-design elements named in the session description so it reads as complete to reviewers and attendees.
A "handout" naturally means the audience-ready document that travels with the deck and includes the standard companion pieces usually circulated with grand rounds materials.
When faculty say they will use "examples," they generally mean built-out teaching cases or mini-scenarios that can anchor discussion on slides and in the audience materials.
A "Friday" delivery means something stable enough to circulate onward without expecting substantial same-day restructuring.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to build a "primer on clinical trial design" for practicing urologists.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 thinks the primer should be a selective, clinician-oriented overview built around a few recurring interpretive issues and 2-3 illustrative urology trials.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 thinks the primer should at least briefly cover each standard component named in the session description—design types, endpoints, participant selection, randomization, sample size, blinding, analysis, pitfalls, and reporting—so it feels complete.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both hear "primer" as meaning introductory and practical, so the phrase creates a natural sense of alignment while hiding a difference in how exhaustive the session must be.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They discuss preparing the "handout" for the session.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a brief learner-facing takeaway, such as a 1-2 page summary or slide printout with key teaching points.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the audience handout bundle that normally accompanies the talk materials, including the printable core slides plus the usual companion items she expects to circulate with the session.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both routinely use the word "handout" in grand rounds planning, and M2 avoids explicitly framing it as an administrative or compliance artifact, so nothing in the wording sounds unusual enough to trigger clarification.

misalignment_points.topic: What examples need to be prepared
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to include a couple of "case examples" to keep the talk practical.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 plans to cite specific published urology trials—such as a landmark prostate cancer RCT and a bladder cancer study—as examples of how design choices affect interpretation.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 expects short teaching cases or mini-scenarios with a clinical setup, a discussion prompt, and a take-home point that can appear in both slides and audience materials.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In educational planning, "case example" comfortably covers both literature examples and teaching scenarios, so each person hears a familiar phrase and assumes the other means the ordinary version they themselves use.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They confirm that materials will be ready "by Friday."
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 thinks success means she can send a content-complete draft Friday evening after clinic, with references, formatting, and packaging still potentially rough.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 thinks success means the materials are review-ready by Friday afternoon and stable enough to circulate immediately without substantive revision.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Date-based planning language often compresses several assumptions—time of day, level of polish, and readiness for onward use—into a single casual phrase, and both apply their own default standard without noticing.
